evaluation.positioning_hook: A Korean-American GBI agent and her blunt Black partner investigate a bakery owner’s fiery death on Buford Highway, where Korean ritual, racial tension, and a possible ghost story collide.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The hook is immediately legible as an investigative mystery with a supernatural edge, and the Buford Highway setting gives it a fresh cultural lane. It’s not four-quadrant, but it has a clear adult audience: crime-thriller viewers who respond to occult-adjacent cases, procedural banter, and culturally specific worlds.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands fast: a woman burns alive in her car outside a Korean bakery, and the GBI is pulled into a case that may involve ritual, omen, or murder. The script keeps returning to the same clean engine — what caused the fire, and what really happened at Happy Cake — which makes the hook easy to explain.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Omar Gaines and Sue Kim are both sharply drawn, with a strong friction-based partnership that gives the investigation personality. Susie Park, Ken Lim, and Jade Han add vivid texture, though the page is still more interested in the case mechanics than in fully deepening everyone’s private lives.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script’s boldest move is treating Korean shamanism, Christian piety, and police procedure as equal parts of the same mystery, then staging the fire sequence like a stylized ritual nightmare. The tonal confidence is real, especially in the transition from grounded interrogation to surreal, music-driven horror imagery.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The investigation moves with purpose from the death scene to the GBI briefing to the bakery interviews to Jade Han, and each stop adds a new layer. The momentum is strongest when the script is gathering clues; it softens a bit in the explanatory dialogue around omens, curses, and ritual history.

resonant_originality.reasoning: This feels like a familiar procedural that has been re-energized by a very specific cultural and geographic world. The combination of Buford Highway, Korean-American family dynamics, and a possible spirit-world explanation gives the premise a memorable identity that is both strange and instantly playable.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: Happy Cake, the 714 group, the Korean-language break room, the mudang ecosystem, and the Buford Highway street-racing corridor all feel story-generating rather than decorative. The world has social hierarchy, cultural codes, and local specificity that can keep producing scenes.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a distinct tonal signature: deadpan cop banter, cultural specificity, and sudden surreal horror imagery. The sound design motifs, ritual music cues, and stylized fire sequence give it a hard-to-mistake identity.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are real seeds of deeper material here — assimilation, faith, shame, class, and the tension between public reputation and private belief. The script hints at a larger emotional and mythic layer, though this draft is still primarily operating as a case-driven mystery.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The Omar/Sue pairing is strong enough to carry the movie, and the bakery staff plus the Park family create a usable web of recurring friction. It’s not an ensemble that generates endless combinations, but it does have enough relational tension to keep scenes alive.

lead_characters.name: Sue Kim
lead_characters.demographics: Korean American woman, 30s, GBI senior special agent.
lead_characters.hook: A hyper-competent, emotionally sealed investigator who moves through rooms like she already knows the answer, but whose Korean background makes her both insider and outsider in the Happy Cake world. She’s dry, controlled, and quietly provocative, with a private history that surfaces through her connection to Jade Han and her fluency in the cultural codes everyone else is trying to decode.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Sandra Oh in Killing Eve — a cool, exacting professional whose restraint is the performance. It gives an actor the chance to play intelligence, authority, and buried personal history while letting the smallest reactions land as story.

lead_characters.name: Omar Gaines
lead_characters.demographics: Black man, 30s, GBI senior special agent, military bearing.
lead_characters.hook: A disciplined, observant investigator who reads the room fast and tries to keep the partnership human with humor and small talk, only to discover Sue Kim is operating on a different frequency. He’s the audience’s entry point into the case’s cultural weirdness, and his grounded professionalism keeps the script from floating away into pure atmosphere.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Mahershala Ali in True Detective season 3 — controlled authority with a private interior life and a partner dynamic that reveals character through friction. It gives an actor the chance to play command, skepticism, and comic exasperation without losing dignity.

lead_characters.name: Susie Park
lead_characters.demographics: Korean woman, 50s, bakery owner and family matriarch.
lead_characters.hook: A status-obsessed, exacting business owner whose vanity and control issues make her instantly legible as a force in the room, even before the fire. She’s the kind of character whose absence still dominates the movie, because every employee and family member is reacting to the pressure she created.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Glenn Close in Fatal Attraction or The Wife — a commanding, difficult woman whose authority is the role. It gives an actor a chance to make a character memorable through posture, bite, and the sense that everyone else has been orbiting her for years.

lead_characters.name: Kyung-ho Lim
lead_characters.hook: The exhausted middle manager trapped between a volatile boss and a staff that reads the world through omens, guilt, and hierarchy. He’s the pressure valve of the bakery scenes, and his nervous diplomacy gives the investigation a human, compromised witness who knows more than he wants to say.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Steven Yeun in Minari or Will Patton in a pressure-cooker ensemble — a man carrying stress in every pause. It gives an actor the chance to play embarrassment, loyalty, and quiet panic in the same scene.

lead_characters.name: Jade Han
lead_characters.hook: A fast-talking, weed-smoking ritual practitioner who treats the spirit world like a lived-in neighborhood and the investigation like a social call. She’s the script’s wild card: funny, slippery, spiritually confident, and just credible enough to make the supernatural lane feel dangerous.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Tilda Swinton in Suspiria or Aunjanue Ellis in The Book of Clarence — a role that can be playful, eerie, and authoritative at once. It gives an actor a big tonal swing and a chance to make exposition feel like a performance event.

lead_characters.name: Soo-yeon Park
lead_characters.hook: A sharp-tongued family gatekeeper who treats the investigation as an intrusion and speaks with the authority of someone used to being obeyed. She’s a great friction character: defensive, proud, and just opaque enough to keep the family’s real story from being cleanly accessible.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Hong Chau in The Whale or Meryl Streep in August: Osage County — a role built on verbal force and emotional resistance. It gives an actor a chance to dominate scenes with precision and contempt.

lead_characters.name: Dr. John Kim
lead_characters.hook: The polished, overextended son trying to manage family reputation, police questions, and his aunt’s temper without ever fully taking control. He reads as the bridge between worlds — professional, assimilated, and visibly uncomfortable with the spiritual and emotional mess around him.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Randall Park in Shortcomings or John Cho in Columbus — a contained, intelligent role where discomfort is the point. It gives an actor the chance to play restraint, embarrassment, and buried authority.

lead_characters.name: Eun-ja
lead_characters.hook: A gossipy, emotionally porous worker who oscillates between piety, superstition, and blunt common sense. She’s one of the script’s best texture characters, because she turns exposition into personality and makes the bakery feel socially alive.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of June Squibb in Nebraska — a role that can steal scenes through specificity, timing, and lived-in contradiction. It gives an actor a chance to be funny, nosy, and oddly moving without ever becoming a stock side character.

lead_characters.name: Mi-sook
lead_characters.hook: A devout, anxious worker whose instinct is to sanctify the boss and interpret every spill, ink mark, and bad feeling as evidence of cosmic order. She’s a perfect counterweight to Eun-ja, and together they create a comic-ritual chorus around the central mystery.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Kathy Bates in a supporting ensemble role — a character who can be funny, severe, and emotionally legible in a single exchange. It gives an actor a chance to build a memorable presence from rhythm and reaction.

lead_characters.name: Young-hee
lead_characters.hook: The youngest worker in the room, eager to please and constantly overcorrecting under the gaze of the older women. She gives the bakery scenes a generational layer and a real sense of hierarchy, because every line she says feels like a test she might fail.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Stephanie Hsu in a smaller ensemble role — a young character whose nervous energy and comic timing make her pop. It gives an actor a chance to play vulnerability, eagerness, and social pressure.

lead_characters.name: Karen Powell
lead_characters.hook: A blunt, physically imposing law-enforcement boss who cuts through bureaucratic fog with pure command energy. She’s a strong authority figure in a room full of men trying to manage optics, and she instantly clarifies the chain of power.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Regina King in a hard-edged authority role — direct, intimidating, and efficient. It gives an actor the chance to own a room with minimal dialogue and maximum presence.

lead_characters.name: Vic Reynolds
lead_characters.hook: A rumpled, awkward administrator who wants the case handled quietly and can barely hide his discomfort while saying it. He’s useful because he embodies the institutional pressure behind the investigation without turning into a cartoon bureaucrat.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of J.K. Simmons in a low-key authority role — a man whose discomfort is part of the character. It gives an actor a chance to play institutional fatigue and dry authority.

lead_characters.name: Joe Reese
lead_characters.hook: A deadpan logistics guy who functions like the case’s human firewall, controlling access and information with clipped efficiency. He’s not flashy, but he gives the investigation a procedural spine and a memorable comic-flat register.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Shea Whigham in a procedural support role — terse, watchful, and oddly funny. It gives an actor the chance to make minimalism feel loaded.

lead_characters.name: Jamal Carter
lead_characters.hook: A seasoned local cop with a storyteller’s instinct and a dry, amused relationship to the absurdity of the case. He’s the kind of supporting role that makes the world feel lived-in because he can deliver exposition without sounding like exposition.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Delroy Lindo in a supporting procedural role — warm, skeptical, and effortlessly watchable. It gives an actor the chance to make a briefing scene feel like a performance.

lead_characters.name: David Pratt
lead_characters.demographics: Black man, 50s, DeKalb County PD major.
lead_characters.hook: A swaggering local authority who needles the state investigators and enjoys the politics of jurisdiction almost as much as the case itself. He adds friction, personality, and a little comic ego to the law-enforcement ecosystem.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Wendell Pierce in a sharp supporting role — confident, funny, and territorial. It gives an actor a chance to play institutional pride with bite.

lead_characters.name: Tom Holt
lead_characters.hook: The tech guy who quietly becomes the bridge between the mystery and the evidence, with just enough personality to keep the lab work from feeling sterile. He’s the practical counterweight to the script’s supernatural speculation.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of David Harbour in a grounded supporting role — smart, slightly rumpled, and useful under pressure. It gives an actor a chance to be the competent guy who still has a personality.

lead_characters.name: Michelle Yoon
lead_characters.hook: A presence more than a speaking character in this draft, but emotionally central to the case because her death becomes the image and wound that the whole story keeps circling. She functions as the haunting center of the mystery, even when she’s only present through memory, footage, and ritual imagery.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a haunting, memory-driven role like the victim presence in The Lovely Bones — brief on dialogue, heavy on emotional imprint. It gives a young actor a chance to make a lasting impression through image and aftermath.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: adult mystery-thriller with supernatural-horror elements, suited to streaming-first or specialty theatrical play.

budget.note: Contemporary locations keep the footprint grounded, but the stylized fire sequence, night exteriors, ritual imagery, and car-burn effects will push this above a bare-bones indie if executed as written.

casting.note: The lead needs an actor who can play procedural authority, dry comedy, and cultural specificity without flattening the role, and the Korean-language ensemble adds a real authenticity requirement across several supporting parts.

development.note: The case is clear, but the script is balancing procedural mystery, family drama, and supernatural suggestion; buyers will want confidence that the fire is being played as a coherent engine rather than a collection of competing explanations.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like elevated mystery-thrillers with a supernatural edge, especially viewers drawn to culturally specific worlds and strong investigator chemistry.
audience_target.demographics: 35-54 skew, slightly female-leaning but not exclusive, urban/suburban adults, genre-literate streaming audience.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary interiors, a limited number of principal locations, and one major stylized fire sequence keep this in indie-feature territory, though the ritual-horror imagery and night work add scope.

lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane where character-forward crime stories are allowed to get weird, but still need a clean hook and a strong lead performance. The Korean-American specificity and the occult-adjacent investigation make it feel premium without requiring tentpole scale.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature with a closed case and no clear sequel or spinoff vector on the page.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Buford Highway gives the mystery a real place.
strengths.what_it_means: The setting is specific enough to feel ownable and commercially legible, which helps the project stand out in a crowded mystery-thriller field. Buyers looking for a fresh regional identity or a culturally textured crime lane will notice it immediately.
strengths.evidence: The script repeatedly grounds the story in Happy Cake Doraville, the Buford Highway corridor, and the street-racing stretch called the Calidad Quarter.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Sue Kim is a strong lead role.
strengths.what_it_means: The role gives a buyer a clear casting target: a smart, controlled investigator with dry humor and buried personal history. That’s the kind of part that can attract a name actress and anchor the whole package.
strengths.evidence: Her deadpan exchanges with Gaines, her instant recognition of Jade Han, and her icy control in the Soo-yeon interview all define her fast.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The procedural and supernatural lanes are fused cleanly.
strengths.what_it_means: The script can be sold as a mystery with a horror charge rather than as a pure genre experiment, which broadens the buyer conversation. That hybrid lane is attractive to streamers and specialty genre financiers who want something elevated but accessible.
strengths.evidence: The investigation moves from CCTV anomalies and forensic speculation into mudang ritual, apparition imagery, and the stylized fire sequence.

strengths.what_it_means: The bakery staff and family scenes create a social world with hierarchy, humor, and cultural specificity, which is valuable both creatively and commercially. It gives the movie a texture that can travel as prestige genre rather than generic occult procedural.
strengths.evidence: Eun-ja, Mi-sook, Young-hee, Soo-yeon, and Dr. Kim all speak in distinct registers and occupy different positions in the bakery ecosystem.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The fire sequence is a signature set piece.
strengths.what_it_means: The stylized ignition and the later surreal replay of the death give the film a trailer-ready image engine. That kind of visual identity helps a buyer see marketing value beyond the page.
strengths.evidence: The script stages Susie’s burning car through CCTV distortion, ritual music, and a giallo-like visual treatment of Michelle’s apparition.

whats_special.headline: This has the kind of specific world and lead role that can make a buyer lean in fast: a Korean-American procedural with a supernatural charge, a memorable Buford Highway setting, and a strong actress-facing part in Sue Kim. The production footprint stays in indie-feature range while the imagery and cultural texture give it a premium, trailer-friendly identity.

items.area: The supernatural rules stay deliberately blurry.
items.detail: The script keeps the fire open to ghost story, ritual curse, and forensic anomaly, which is part of the appeal but also the main buyer question. In a greenlight conversation, that ambiguity will read as either sophisticated or unresolved depending on who’s in the room.

items.area: The exposition leans hard on explanation scenes.
items.detail: A lot of the case information arrives through briefing-room dialogue, witness recaps, and cultural translation rather than through active discovery. That makes the script clear, but it also concentrates momentum in talk-heavy stretches that will be watched closely in development.

The movie’s appeal rises or falls on the lead performance because Sue is the clearest star-facing role and the emotional anchor for the investigation. That’s a strength, but it also narrows the casting conversation to actors who can play cool authority without flattening the humor.

items.area: The fire effects need disciplined scope control.
items.detail: The car-burn sequence, CCTV distortion, apparition imagery, and ritualized replay of the death all ask for more than a simple practical approach. If the visual language gets expensive, the project can drift above its indie-feature lane quickly.

issues.headline: The main friction is not the premise — it’s the balance between procedural clarity and supernatural ambiguity, which the script intentionally keeps unresolved. Add the fact that the lead role has to carry the whole package and the fire imagery needs real visual discipline, and those are the conversations a producer will have before saying yes.
